title: What is a transport management system (TMS)? A practical guide
summary: A transport management system (TMS) plans, dispatches, tracks and bills road transport. What it does, who needs one, and how to choose one.
body_markdown:
## What a TMS is


A transport management system, or TMS, is software that manages the movement of goods by road, from the moment an order is ready to ship until the delivery is confirmed and invoiced. It is also called a transportation management system, or transportation management software.


It sits between the systems that create orders, such as an ERP or a warehouse management system, and the people who move them: planners, dispatchers, drivers and carriers.


## What a TMS does


Most systems cover the same four jobs, in the order a delivery happens.


1. **Plan.** Group orders into routes that respect delivery time windows, vehicle capacity and driver hours.
2. **Dispatch.** Assign each route to a vehicle of your own fleet or to a carrier, and send it to the driver’s phone.
3. **Track.** Follow each delivery in real time, and collect the proof of delivery when it is done.
4. **Bill.** Work out what each delivery costs, check carrier invoices against the agreed rates, and invoice your customers.


## Who needs one


A spreadsheet works for a handful of deliveries a day. It stops working when the number of orders, vehicles or carriers grows. A TMS is worth looking at if you recognise several of these situations:


- Planning tomorrow’s routes takes hours and depends on one person.
- Customers call to ask where their delivery is.
- Proofs of delivery are on paper and come back days later.
- You cannot say what a given delivery, route or customer costs you.
- You work with several carriers, and each one reports in its own way.


This applies to manufacturers and other shippers, to distributors and retailers, and to logistics providers who move goods for others.


## TMS, ERP and WMS: how they fit together


The three are often confused. An ERP records orders, stock and accounting. A warehouse management system (WMS) runs what happens inside the warehouse. A TMS takes over at the dock door and runs what happens on the road. It does not replace the other two: it receives orders from them and sends back delivery statuses and costs.


## What to look for when choosing


- **Your own fleet and your carriers in one place.** Most companies use both, and planning them separately hides the cheapest option.
- **A driver app that works on any phone.** If drivers need special hardware, carriers will not use it.
- **Connections to what you already have.** Orders should arrive from your ERP or WMS, and positions from the GPS units already in the trucks.
- **Time to go live.** Ask how long a comparable company took, in weeks, and what it had to prepare.
- **Fit with your countries.** Languages, documents and local rules differ from one market to the next.


## Where AI changes things


Planning is where software helps most. An optimiser can compare far more route combinations than a person can in the same time. Newer systems also use AI to read orders from emails and documents, to flag deliveries at risk of being late, and to explain where transport costs come from. The planner still decides; the system does the calculating.
